title: Peacocks and cranes
hook: the monks' monsoon poems: clouds, peacocks crying, cranes flying home

segments.voice: Yesterday, Subhuti's hut was roofed, and he told the sky to go ahead. Your line was rain if you like. What came down on you, and did the line help? Today, the rain arrives, and the birds come with it. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

Dark clouds stack up over the hills. Thunder. A flash of white as birds lift off a riverbank. In the trees, a peacock cries out. Some of the brothers' songs begin right there, at the edge of the rains. The poets aren't describing the weather to pass the time. They're telling us where they sat, and what the season did to the mind. Today, two birds from those rain songs, and what the monks did when the sky opened.
screen: `CLOUDS OVER THE HILLS.` → `A PEACOCK CRIES OUT.` → `WHAT THE MONKS DID WITH IT.`

segments.voice: First, the peacocks. In one elder's verses, peacocks with fine crests and blue necks cry out in the woods, the sky rumbles, and the wide earth is soaked with new rain. And then he says: this is the time to meditate. The noise isn't a distraction. It's a signal. Second, the cranes. Another elder, Sappaka, watches a crane with bright white wings take flight from a black storm cloud, afraid of it, looking for shelter. And he says that then the river Ajakarani delights him. He comes back to that line again and again, as the birds come and go, almost like a song's refrain. Third, the season itself. When the rains come, roads turn to mud, and tradition says the Buddha asked the monks to stop wandering for the rainy months and stay in one place. That stay is called vassa, the rains retreat. So the monsoon poems are poems of staying put. The clouds move, the birds move, the river rises. The monk doesn't go anywhere. Fourth, what these two poems leave out. They don't call the storm holy, and they don't call it a trap. They don't argue with it. They watch. A bird flies for cover. A river runs high. A man under a roof hears it all and settles a little deeper. The rains came. That's the whole report, and for these elders it was enough to begin.
screen: `PEACOCKS CRY: TIME TO MEDITATE.` · `A WHITE CRANE FLEES THE BLACK CLOUD.` · `VASSA: STAY PUT FOR THE RAINS.` · `THEY DON'T ARGUE. THEY WATCH.` · then, large: `THE RAINS CAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch the weather. Go to a window, or step outside, or just close your eyes and feel the air on your skin. What's the sky doing? Clouds, sun, wind, rain, or nothing much at all. Don't call it good or bad. Just watch it the way the elders watched the cranes. If a bird crosses, follow it until it's gone. If a sound comes, a car, a gust, a door, let it be the peacock's cry: a signal to come back to the breath. And stay where you are. The bell holds the time.
Peacocks and cranes. The birds of the brothers' rain songs: peacocks crying as the clouds come in, a white crane flying for shelter ahead of the storm. Today's word.
Your line: the rains came. Today, when the weather turns, or your day does, stay put for one breath before you move. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Theravada monks and nuns still keep the rains retreat, vassa, staying in one monastery for the rainy season, and lay people often visit them then with food and robes.

original.note: Pali: vassa, the rains, and the rains retreat when monks stay in one place.

trapdoor: what you thought: nature poems about pretty birds.
what it means: the elders' rain songs: the clouds come, the birds move, and the monk stays and sits.
what a scholar hears: Sappaka's refrain names the river Ajakarani; and the rains retreat, vassa, is what kept the monks in one place to watch.

sources.ref: Theragatha, Culaka (vv. 211–212: peacocks crying, the time to meditate)
Theragatha, Sappaka (vv. 307–310: the crane, the black cloud, the river Ajakarani)

notes: All verses paraphrased; no translation quoted.

Peacock verses: attributed to Culaka (Thag vv. 211–212 in PTS numbering, as remembered); the elder is left unnamed in the voice. Confirm the reference and the paraphrase (crested, blue-necked peacocks crying; sky rumbling; earth soaked; 'a time to meditate').
Crane verses: Sappaka (Thag vv. 307–310 as remembered): a crane with white wings flees a black cloud seeking shelter, and 'then the river Ajakarani delights me' as a refrain.
Rains retreat attributed to tradition (Vinaya Mahavagga 3); confirm. howItsDone describes current Theravada practice; confirm.
Editor: softened 'several of the brothers' songs' to 'some', and limited 'they never call the storm holy or a trap' to these two poems, so no count or sweeping claim about the whole book.
Auditor (fresh review): read in full against the Pali and nearby days; no changes needed.
